To capture an image on film you expose the film to the ambient light. the length of that exposure is called 'exposure' (oddly enough). Every object is a light source. A dim object will take longer exposure to register on the film, when compared to a brighter object. The earth from the moon is a big bright ball against a black background. That black background has a bunch of dots of light. To capture the little dots of light requires a longer exposure, because they are comparatively dim w regards to the Earth. To get both the earth and stars in the same shot you have to make some decisions. Either the earth is going to be a blown out white blob because it has been over exposed or you can switch to a faster film. But that comes w tradeoffs too. Faster film is more sensitive to light, so you can work in low light. But traditionally you gave up some resolution. The pictures appear to have a grain to them.

So all of that is a balancing act. How long can you expose the film and capture the earth in detail is a much shorter time than that needed to get the stars too. And you have to account for that black background of space AND the very bright surface of the moon as well.

That's a long winded way of saying the earth would be over exposed if you could see the stars too.
